A container is a process

Docker starts a program for you. Find that program on the machine, and see the one thing that makes it different from every other program running there.

The problem

On your phone, every app you open runs as a process: a running program, with its own memory. You have used Docker at work, typed docker run, and heard that your program now runs "in Docker". Is it inside a small computer inside yours? A special kind of program? Something Docker runs by itself?

The answer decides how you debug it. When your program won’t start under Docker, or gets killed, you need to know whose rules apply and where to look. This module answers the question from the bottom up, with real output from a real machine.

See it

The building block

Every program on a Linux machine, from your shell to a database server, is run by the kernel: the core of the operating system. It is the one program that runs all the others: it gives each one its turns on the processor, its memory and its files. On servers, and on Android phones, that kernel is Linux.

When the kernel starts a process, it gives it a number, its PID (process ID). ps is a small program that prints the processes the kernel is running, one line each, with their PIDs.

Now docker run alpine:3.20 sleep 1000. sleep 1000 is a tiny program that waits 1000 seconds and exits. alpine:3.20 is a container image, an image for short: a package of the files a program needs to start, here the files of Alpine, a small Linux distribution, and the program sleep among them. Docker unpacks the image's files and asks the kernel to start sleep from them.

On the host, the machine Docker runs on, ps then shows one more line: sleep 1000, with PID 3393. It sits in the same list as bash and ps, numbered by the same kernel. No second operating system started; nothing sits between sleep and the kernel. Docker set the process up and then stepped aside.

So what is different? Run ps again, but inside the container, with docker exec box ps (docker exec runs one more program in a container that is already running, here the one named box). It lists two processes: sleep and itself. The kernel hides every other process from it. A container is exactly that: an ordinary process, or a few of them, that the kernel runs inside a fence. The fence limits what the process can see (other processes, the host's files, the network) and how much it can use (memory, processor time). The next puzzles take the fence apart, one piece at a time.

Two things a container is not:

  • It is not a copy of Docker running your program. Docker asked the kernel to start the process; the kernel runs it.
  • It is not the image. The image is files; nothing runs until a process starts from them. Ten containers from one image are ten processes.

The analogy

An apartment block. The caretaker, the kernel, runs the whole building: water, power, keys, for everyone. Each household is a process. A container is a household in a flat with frosted windows and its own meter: it can't see the neighbours, it can draw only so much power, but it lives in the same building and calls the same caretaker as everyone else.

Run it yourself

Before you start

Every Run it yourself in this course needs a Linux machine with Docker Engine, where you can also look at the host's side: its process list, its files.

  • On Linux, install Docker Engine for your distribution with Docker's instructions (docs.docker.com/engine/install).
  • On a Mac or a Windows laptop, Docker Desktop runs the docker commands, but hides the Linux host they run on (puzzle 1 shows why). To see both sides, make yourself a small Ubuntu machine with a tool such as Multipass, and install Docker Engine inside it.
  • The docker command needs root's rights: put sudo in front of it, or add your user to the docker group (Docker's post-installation steps show how). Docker warns that "the docker group grants root-level privileges to the user", which puzzle 5 explains.
  • If every docker command prints "permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock", Docker is running but your user may not use it: use sudo, or log out and in again after joining the group.

The commands

On a Linux machine with Docker installed. Before you run the third command, write down how many lines it will print, and whether the second command will find sleep at all.

docker run -d --name box alpine:3.20 sleep 1000
ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd | grep "[s]leep 1000"
docker exec box ps -o pid,args
docker rm -f box

-d starts the container in the background, and --name names it box. ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd prints every process with its PID, its parent's PID (the process that started it) and its command; the brackets in [s]leep stop grep from finding its own line. This is the output from the run behind this page (your PIDs will differ):

7cd6333d62bd685fb0432cc58d8b24f77fdd707db35f9573b85d9de4723ce1bb
 3393  3367 sleep 1000
PID   COMMAND
    1 sleep 1000
    7 ps -o pid,args

The first line is the new container's ID. Inside, the numbers are different: sleep is 1 there, not 3393. Puzzle 2 shows why one process has two numbers. On a Mac or a Windows laptop, and with Docker Desktop even on Linux, the second command finds nothing: puzzle 1 shows where the process really runs.

Check yourself

You start two containers from the same image, each running sleep 1000. How many sleep processes does the host's ps list?

Not quite. Each docker run starts its own process; the image is only files, and nothing in it runs by itself. Re-read that part ↑

Right. Two processes: one per container, both on the host's list.

Not quite. The kernel runs a container's program like any other process, and ps lists it.

A second container, web, also runs sleep 1000 on the same machine. How many sleep lines does docker exec box ps print?

Not quite. The kernel hides every process outside box's fence, other containers' included.

Right. Each container sees only its own processes.

Not quite. It sees its own container's processes: sleep and itself.

The kernel ends the process with PID 3393, for example to free memory. What is left of the container's program?

Not quite. Docker asked the kernel to start the process and stepped aside; the kernel runs it. Re-read that part ↑

Right. The container's program is that one process.

Not quite. An image is files; nothing runs from it until a process starts.

Sources
  • Docker docs: What is a container? ("A container is an ordinary process on your computer, such as a Node.js server, that runs in isolation."; "its own kernel, the core of the operating system that talks to the hardware"; "An image is a package of everything a container needs to start: the operating system files, the language runtime, the app’s dependencies and code, and settings such as which command to run.")
  • Docker docs: Docker Engine security ("When you start a container with docker run , behind the scenes Docker creates a set of namespaces and control groups for the container."; "Processes running within a container cannot see, and even less affect, processes running in another container, or in the host system.")
  • Docker docs: Install Docker Engine ("This section describes how to install Docker Engine on Linux.")
  • Docker docs: Linux post-installation steps for Docker Engine ("By default it's the root user that owns the Unix socket, and other users can only access it using sudo ."; "The docker group grants root-level privileges to the user.")
  • Multipass documentation ("Multipass is a tool to generate cloud-style virtual machines (VMs) quickly on Linux, macOS and Windows.")
  • Linux manual: credentials(7) ("Each process has a unique nonnegative integer identifier that is assigned when the process is created using fork(2).")
  • Linux manual: getpid(2) ("getpid() returns the process ID (PID) of the calling process.")
  • The output under Run it yourself, and the PIDs in the diagram (bash 3633, ps 3635, sleep 3393), were produced in this session (the permission denied message as UID 1000 without the docker group) with Docker Engine 29.9.2 on the test machine (Ubuntu 24.04 userland in a Firecracker microVM, custom kernel 6.18.44, cgroup v1), image alpine:3.20.

What you now know

A container is an ordinary process, started from an image's files, that the kernel runs like any other one; the host's ps lists it with its own PID. What makes it a container is a fence the kernel puts around it, limiting what it can see and how much it can use.
